A massive spin-1/2 fermion $X$ decays at rest into three massless fermions,
$X\to A+B+C$, where $A$ and $C$ are outgoing fermions and $B$ is an outgoing
antifermion. At a fixed phase-space point the decay produces a pure three-qubit
state in the helicity basis of the three final particles. The structure of that

# From Four-Fermion Decay Operators to Tripartite Bell Nonlocality

## Problem background

A massive spin-1/2 fermion $X$ decays at rest into three massless fermions,
$X\to A+B+C$, where $A$ and $C$ are outgoing fermions and $B$ is an outgoing
antifermion. At a fixed phase-space point the decay produces a pure three-qubit
state in the helicity basis of the three final particles. The structure of that
state — and therefore its multipartite entanglement and its ability to violate
tripartite Bell inequalities — is controlled by the Lorentz structure of the
four-fermion contact interaction driving the decay.

This is a closed-book analytic–numerical task. Everything needed to define the
targets is stated below; no external literature is required or permitted as a
source of final formulas. You must derive six load-bearing analytic results,
implement a general numerical solver, and package both according to the exact
output contract in this document.

> **Closed-book rule (binding).** Work only from this document and your own
> reasoning and computation. Do NOT access the network for any purpose: do not
> search the web, do not download or fetch papers, preprints, datasets, or
> code, and do not call any external API or model. Do not use `curl`, `wget`,
> `pip install` from remote indexes, `git clone`, or any browser/search tool.
> All derivations must be your own; all required numerical libraries (numpy,
> and optionally scipy) are already available in the environment. Retrieving
> the source paper, a published result, or any external solution is a
> disqualifying violation of the task.

## Scientific objective

For scalar, vector, and tensor four-fermion interactions:

1. derive the helicity amplitudes and the normalized three-qubit helicity
   state at an arbitrary phase-space point;
2. derive the entanglement structure (pairwise concurrences, one-to-rest
   concurrences, three-tangle $\tau$, and the concurrence-triangle measure
   $F_3$);
3. analytically reduce and then numerically optimize the Mermin, Svetlichny,
   and tight $4\times4\times2$ Bell observables;
4. implement a general solver that evaluates all of these quantities for
   hidden kinematic and coupling configurations supplied at verification time.

Your submission must not rely on hard-coded rows, memorized output tables, or
branching on case identifiers. The verifier runs your solver on fresh hidden
inputs and rejects confirmed lookup behavior.

## Kinematics

Work in the rest frame of $X$: $p_X^\mu=(m,0,0,0)$. Set $m=1$ in numerical
work. The decay plane is the $x$–$z$ plane:

$$
p_A^\mu=p_A(1,0,0,1),\qquad
p_B^\mu=p_B(1,\sin\theta_B,0,\cos\theta_B),\qquad
p_C^\mu=p_C(1,-\sin\theta_C,0,\cos\theta_C).
$$

Energy–momentum conservation fixes

$$
p_A=-mD\sin(\theta_B+\theta_C),\qquad
p_B=mD\sin\theta_C,\qquad
p_C=mD\sin\theta_B,\qquad
D=\frac{1}{\sin\theta_B+\sin\theta_C-\sin(\theta_B+\theta_C)} .
$$

All evaluated configurations lie in the nonsingular physical interior

$$
0<\theta_B,\theta_C<\pi,\qquad \pi<\theta_B+\theta_C<2\pi .
$$

The initial spin-polarization direction of $X$ is
$\boldsymbol n=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ \sin\theta\sin\phi,\ \cos\theta)$.

## Dirac and spinor conventions

These conventions are binding; every convention-sensitive choice below is part
of the target definition. Use

$$
g_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1),\qquad
\epsilon^{0123}=+1,\qquad \epsilon_{0123}=-1 .
$$

Dirac representation:

$$
\gamma^0=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf 1_2&0\\0&-\mathbf 1_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\gamma^i=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_i\\-\sigma_i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\gamma^5=i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3,
$$

$$
P_L=\frac{1-\gamma^5}{2},\qquad P_R=\frac{1+\gamma^5}{2},\qquad
\sigma^{\mu\nu}=\frac{i}{2}[\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu],\qquad
\sigma_{\mu\nu}=g_{\mu\alpha}g_{\nu\beta}\sigma^{\alpha\beta} .
$$

Repeated Lorentz indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.

For a momentum direction
$\widehat{\boldsymbol p}=(\sin\vartheta\cos\varphi_p,\
\sin\vartheta\sin\varphi_p,\ \cos\vartheta)$ define the helicity two-spinors

$$
\chi_+(\vartheta,\varphi_p)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\vartheta/2)\\
e^{i\varphi_p}\sin(\vartheta/2)\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\chi_-(\vartheta,\varphi_p)=\begin{pmatrix}-e^{-i\varphi_p}\sin(\vartheta/2)\\
\cos(\vartheta/2)\end{pmatrix},
$$

so that $(\widehat{\boldsymbol p}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)\chi_\lambda
=\lambda\chi_\lambda$ with $\lambda=\pm1$. Use the massless spinors

$$
u(p,\lambda)=\sqrt E\begin{pmatrix}\chi_\lambda\\ \lambda\chi_\lambda
\end{pmatrix},\qquad
v(p,\lambda)=\sqrt E\begin{pmatrix}\chi_{-\lambda}\\ -\lambda\chi_{-\lambda}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Particle $B$ is the outgoing antifermion and is represented by
$v_B(p_B,\lambda_B)$. The incoming polarized rest-frame spinor is

$$
u_X(\boldsymbol n)=\sqrt{2m}\,
\big(\cos(\theta/2),\ e^{i\phi}\sin(\theta/2),\ 0,\ 0\big)^T ,
$$

and $\bar u=u^\dagger\gamma^0$, $\bar v=v^\dagger\gamma^0$. For the three
outgoing momenta use the literal direction angles

$$
(\vartheta_A,\varphi_A)=(0,0),\qquad
(\vartheta_B,\varphi_B)=(\theta_B,0),\qquad
(\vartheta_C,\varphi_C)=(\theta_C,\pi).
$$

Use these azimuths as literal constants; do not reconstruct them from momentum
components.

## Four-fermion interactions

All couplings are real numbers.

Scalar:

$$
\mathcal O_S=\left[\bar\psi_A(c_S+ic_A\gamma^5)\psi_X\right]
\left[\bar\psi_C(d_S+id_A\gamma^5)\psi_B\right].
$$

Vector:

$$
\mathcal O_V=\left[\bar\psi_A\gamma_\mu(c_LP_L+c_RP_R)\psi_X\right]
\left[\bar\psi_C\gamma^\mu(d_LP_L+d_RP_R)\psi_B\right].
$$

Tensor:

$$
\mathcal O_T=\left[\bar\psi_A(c_M+ic_E\gamma^5)\sigma^{\mu\nu}\psi_X\right]
\left[\bar\psi_C(d_M+id_E\gamma^5)\sigma_{\mu\nu}\psi_B\right].
$$

Any overall EFT coefficient common to all helicity amplitudes of one
interaction cancels after normalization and may be dropped.

## Helicity state and basis ordering

For interaction $I\in\{S,V,T\}$ compute
$\mathcal M^I_{\lambda_A\lambda_B\lambda_C}$ directly from the spinor
contractions and construct

$$
|\Psi_I\rangle=\frac{1}{\mathcal N_I}
\sum_{\lambda_A\lambda_B\lambda_C}
\mathcal M^I_{\lambda_A\lambda_B\lambda_C}
|\lambda_A\lambda_B\lambda_C\rangle,
\qquad
\mathcal N_I^2=\sum_{\lambda_A\lambda_B\lambda_C}
\big|\mathcal M^I_{\lambda_A\lambda_B\lambda_C}\big|^2 .
$$

Identify $|+\rangle\equiv|0\rangle$ and $|-\rangle\equiv|1\rangle$. The
eight-dimensional ordering is

$$
|{+}{+}{+}\rangle,\ |{+}{+}{-}\rangle,\ |{+}{-}{+}\rangle,\ |{+}{-}{-}\rangle,\
|{-}{+}{+}\rangle,\ |{-}{+}{-}\rangle,\ |{-}{-}{+}\rangle,\ |{-}{-}{-}\rangle ,
$$

i.e. component index $=4b(\lambda_A)+2b(\lambda_B)+b(\lambda_C)$ with
$b(+)=0$, $b(-)=1$. Two unnormalized amplitude vectors differing by one common
nonzero complex factor are physically equivalent; a normalized state is defined
up to a global phase.

## Quantum-information definitions

Pauli matrices in the declared computational basis:

$$
\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For $\rho=|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|$ define the correlation tensor

$$
T_{ijk}=\operatorname{Tr}\big[\rho\,\sigma_i\otimes\sigma_j\otimes\sigma_k\big],
\qquad i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\},
$$

with subsystem index order $(i,j,k)\leftrightarrow(A,B,C)$.

Two-qubit concurrence of a reduced state $\rho_{IJ}$: with
$\widetilde\rho_{IJ}=(\sigma_2\otimes\sigma_2)\rho_{IJ}^*
(\sigma_2\otimes\sigma_2)$ (conjugation in the declared basis) and
$r_1\ge r_2\ge r_3\ge r_4\ge0$ the eigenvalues of
$\rho_{IJ}\widetilde\rho_{IJ}$ (tiny negative roundoff clipped),

$$
C_{IJ}=\max\big(0,\ \sqrt{r_1}-\sqrt{r_2}-\sqrt{r_3}-\sqrt{r_4}\big).
$$

One-to-rest concurrence of the pure three-qubit state:

$$
C_{A(BC)}=\sqrt{2\big(1-\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2\big)},\qquad
\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_{BC}\,\rho ,
$$

and cyclically for $C_{B(AC)}$, $C_{C(AB)}$. Three-tangle:

$$
\tau=C_{A(BC)}^2-C_{AB}^2-C_{AC}^2 ,
$$

with values in $[-10^{-12},0]$ clipped to zero. Concurrence-triangle measure:

$$
Q=\frac{C_{A(BC)}+C_{B(AC)}+C_{C(AB)}}{2},\qquad
F_3=\frac{4}{\sqrt3}\sqrt{Q\big(Q-C_{A(BC)}\big)\big(Q-C_{B(AC)}\big)
\big(Q-C_{C(AB)}\big)} ,
$$

with a radicand in $[-10^{-12},0]$ clipped to zero.

## Bell observables

For a real unit vector $\boldsymbol a$ write $A_r=\boldsymbol
A_r\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$, and similarly $B_s$, $C_t$. Every reported Bell
value is the maximum of the absolute expectation value over all measurement
axes.

Mermin:

$$
\mathcal B_M=A_1B_1C_2+A_1B_2C_1+A_2B_1C_1-A_2B_2C_2,\qquad
B_M^{\max}(\rho)=\max\big|\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,\mathcal B_M)\big| ,
$$

with bounds $B_M^{\rm FLR}\le2$ (fully local) and $B_M^{\rm QM}\le4$.

Svetlichny:

$$
\mathcal B_S=A_1B_1C_1+A_1B_1C_2+A_1B_2C_1+A_2B_1C_1
-A_2B_2C_2-A_2B_2C_1-A_2B_1C_2-A_1B_2C_2 ,
$$

with bounds $B_S^{\rm BLR}\le4$ (biseparable) and $B_S^{\rm QM}\le4\sqrt2$.

Tight $4\times4\times2$ operator, for four settings on the first two listed
parties and two settings on the third:

$$
\mathcal B_{442}^{AB|C}
=\big[A_1(B_1+B_2)+A_2(B_1-B_2)\big](C_1+C_2)
+\big[A_3(B_3+B_4)+A_4(B_3-B_4)\big](C_1-C_2).
$$

Define the optimized values $B_{442}^{AB|C}$, $B_{442}^{AC|B}$,
$B_{442}^{BC|A}$ by the corresponding particle assignments (the party after
the bar is the two-setting observer; assignments must be implemented by
consistent permutation of the tensor indices, not by independent formulas),
and

$$
B_{442}^{\rm sym}=\max\big(B_{442}^{AB|C},B_{442}^{AC|B},B_{442}^{BC|A}\big),
$$

with bounds $B_{442}^{\rm FLR}\le4$ and $B_{442}^{\rm QM}\le8$.

## Analytic checkpoints

Six checkpoints are scored, each binary: a checkpoint earns credit only when
its complete final formula bundle is correct AND all of its mandatory bridge
obligations are present, valid, and non-circular. Partial correctness within a
checkpoint earns nothing. C1 and C6 are mandatory load-bearing checkpoints:
failing either caps the final score at 59.

### C1. Vector helicity amplitudes (mandatory)

Starting from $\mathcal O_V$: derive all nonzero helicity amplitudes; prove
that all other helicity configurations vanish in the massless limit; give the
resulting unnormalized four-component amplitude vector up to one common
nonzero complex factor; construct the normalized state in the declared
eight-dimensional ordering.

Mandatory bridges: (1) explicitly evaluate at least one nonzero product of
spinor currents; (2) use chiral projectors and the massless helicity structure
to justify the complete vanishing set.

### C2. Scalar-channel structure

Starting from $\mathcal O_S$: derive all nonzero helicity amplitudes;
determine the separability class; derive an explicit tensor-product
representation if one exists; derive the pairwise concurrences, one-to-rest
concurrences, $\tau$, and $F_3$.

Mandatory bridges: (1) write a coefficient matrix across a relevant
bipartition; (2) establish factorization or non-factorization by an explicit
rank, determinant, or equivalent Schmidt argument.

### C3. Tensor-channel structure

Starting from $\mathcal O_T$: derive all nonzero helicity amplitudes; classify
the state; derive the pairwise and one-to-rest concurrences; derive $\tau$ and
$F_3$.

Mandatory bridges: (1) explain the helicity selection that removes the other
six basis states; (2) explicitly compute at least one single-qubit reduced
density matrix.

### C4. Entanglement of the generic vector state

Write the normalized vector-channel state in terms of its four nonzero complex
coefficients and derive closed forms for $C_{AB}$, $C_{AC}$, $C_{BC}$,
$C_{A(BC)}$, $C_{B(AC)}$, $C_{C(AB)}$, $\tau$, and $F_3$.

Mandatory bridges: (1) explicitly calculate at least one two-qubit reduced
density matrix; (2) explicitly apply the Wootters construction or the CKW
relation — merely naming it is insufficient.

### C5. Partial analytic optimization of Mermin and Svetlichny

Starting from the explicit Bell operators and $T_{ijk}$: isolate Alice's two
measurement vectors; maximize analytically over them; reduce each problem to a
numerical optimization over Bob's and Charlie's four unit vectors.

Mandatory bridges: (1) explicitly derive the two three-vectors multiplying
Alice's axes; (2) justify the maximization via the maximum of a linear
functional on the unit sphere.

### C6. Semi-analytic optimization of B_442 (mandatory)

Starting from the ten-axis definition: introduce normalized sum/difference
vectors; analytically optimize all variables except one orthonormal pair;
reduce the outer search to three angular variables; derive the eigenvalue
expression; retain the outer maximization over the orthonormal pair; derive
the quantum upper bound 8.

Mandatory bridges: (1) correctly construct the two contracted $3\times3$
matrices associated with the two orthogonal directions of the two-setting
observer; (2) explicitly use Rayleigh–Ritz or an equivalent eigenvalue
variational argument to obtain the two largest eigenvalues.

## ANALYSIS.md requirements

Write your derivations to `/app/outputs/ANALYSIS.md` with EXACTLY the
following six top-level sections, in order, with these titles:

```markdown
# C1 Vector helicity amplitudes
# C2 Scalar-channel structure
# C3 Tensor-channel structure
# C4 Entanglement of the generic vector state
# C5 Partial analytic optimization of Mermin and Svetlichny
# C6 Semi-analytic optimization of B_442
```

Each section must contain the subsections `## Starting point`,
`## Mandatory bridge 1`, `## Mandatory bridge 2`, `## Final derived formula`,
`## Consistency check`, and `## Machine-readable certificate`, and the
following marker blocks (shown for C1; use the matching checkpoint id):

- `<!-- BRIDGE:C1:1:BEGIN -->` … `<!-- BRIDGE:C1:1:END -->` around bridge 1;
- `<!-- BRIDGE:C1:2:BEGIN -->` … `<!-- BRIDGE:C1:2:END -->` around bridge 2;
- `<!-- CHECKPOINT:C1:FINAL:BEGIN -->` … `<!-- CHECKPOINT:C1:FINAL:END -->`
  around the final formula bundle;
- `<!-- CHECKPOINT:C1:CONSISTENCY:BEGIN -->` …
  `<!-- CHECKPOINT:C1:CONSISTENCY:END -->` around the consistency check;
- `<!-- CHECKPOINT:C1:CERT:BEGIN -->` … `<!-- CHECKPOINT:C1:CERT:END -->`
  around one fenced ```json code block holding the machine-readable
  certificate.

Formal requirements, enforced mechanically:

1. Each marker pair must appear exactly once; duplicated or unbalanced markers
   invalidate the checkpoint.
2. Formulas must be text/LaTeX, never images. Every FINAL block and every
   BRIDGE block must contain at least one display equation
   (`$$ … $$` or `\[ … \]`) containing an `=` sign, with real mathematical
   content — bridges must show actual equations or algebraic transformations,
   not keywords.
3. The final formula of a checkpoint may not be assumed as its starting point;
   bridge blocks must contain the intermediate objects listed in the
   certificate schemas below.
4. Each consistency check must apply at least one of: normalization, symmetry,
   separable limit, GHZ limit, Bell bound, or direct substitution, and must
   include one fenced ```json block of the form
   `{"type": "<one of: normalization|symmetry|separable_limit|ghz_limit|bell_bound|direct_substitution>", "lhs": <number>, "rhs": <number>}`
   whose two numbers agree to within $10^{-6}$ (relative or absolute).
5. `ANALYSIS.md` must not exceed 5 MB.

## Machine-readable certificates

Because grading is deterministic, each checkpoint's final formulas and bridge
artifacts must also be supplied as machine-checkable expressions inside the
CERT block. The verifier evaluates your expressions at hidden generic points
and compares them with an independent reference implementation. Expressions
that fail to parse, reference undeclared names, or error/overflow at any valid
probe point score zero for that checkpoint.

### Expression language

Expressions are single-line Python-syntax strings. Allowed: numbers, the
declared variable names, parentheses, `+ - * / **`, whitespace, and calls to
the allowed functions. Character set: letters, digits, `_ + - * / ( ) , .`
and whitespace (space or tab). No indexing/brackets, no attribute access, no
double underscores, no strings. Maximum 4096 characters per expression.

Scalar functions: `sin`, `cos`, `exp`, `sqrt`, `conjugate`, `Abs`; constants
`I` (imaginary unit) and `pi`. All arithmetic is complex; `sqrt` is the
principal complex square root; `Abs` returns a real number.

In addition to the per-checkpoint variables listed below, the convention
constant `m` (bound to $1$) and the on-shell momentum magnitudes `pA`, `pB`,
`pC` (the $p_A,p_B,p_C$ of the kinematics section, functions of
$\theta_B,\theta_C$) are bound in every certificate expression. You may write
amplitude expressions either in reduced form (angles/couplings only) or with
explicit mass/momentum factors; amplitude vectors are compared projectively,
so any overall factor cancels.

Array helpers (available only where stated): for a rank-$n$ array `X`, a
3-vector `v`, and 3×3 matrices `M`, `N`:

- `contract(X, v, axis)`: contract index `axis` (0-based) of `X` with `v`;
  e.g. `contract(T, v, 2)` is the 3×3 matrix $\sum_k T_{ijk}v_k$, and
  `contract(M, v, 1)` is the 3-vector $\sum_j M_{ij}v_j$.
- `matmul(M, N)`: matrix product; `transpose(M)`: matrix transpose.
- `norm(v)`: Euclidean norm; `dot(u, v)`: real dot product;
  `cross(u, v)`: cross product.
- `sum_top_eigs(M, k)`: sum of the `k` largest eigenvalues of the symmetric
  matrix `M` (the argument must be symmetric to $10^{-9}$).
- `sqrt`, `Abs` also apply to real scalars in this context.

Neutral worked example (no relation to this task): a certificate field for a
point-charge field magnitude could be `"E": "q/(4*pi*eps*r**2)"`; a vector
certificate built from a matrix `M` and vector `v` could be
`"w": "contract(M, v, 1)"`, meaning $w_i=\sum_j M_{ij}v_j$.

### Helicity labels

Helicity configurations are three-character strings over `+`/`-` in the order
$(\lambda_A,\lambda_B,\lambda_C)$, e.g. `"+-+"` means $\lambda_A=+1,
\lambda_B=-1,\lambda_C=+1$.

### C1 certificate schema

Variables: `thB, thC, th, phi, cL, cR, dL, dR` (angles in radians), plus the
always-bound `m, pA, pB, pC` described above (the bridge-1 spinor-current
components are naturally written with these momentum factors).

```json
{
  "checkpoint": "C1",
  "amplitudes": {"<all 8 helicity labels>": "<scalar expr; write 0 for vanishing components>"},
  "bridge1": {
    "helicity": "<one label with nonzero amplitude at generic couplings>",
    "current_AX": ["<expr mu=0>", "<expr mu=1>", "<expr mu=2>", "<expr mu=3>"],
    "current_CB": ["<expr mu=0>", "<expr mu=1>", "<expr mu=2>", "<expr mu=3>"]
  },
  "bridge2": {
    "mechanisms": {"<all 8 labels>": "<one of: nonzero | first_bilinear_vanishes | second_bilinear_vanishes | lorentz_contraction_vanishes>"}
  }
}
```

`amplitudes` is graded per hidden point by projective fidelity of the full
8-component vector against the reference (one common complex factor allowed),
plus exact agreement of the zero set. `current_AX` and `current_CB` are the
contravariant components of $\bar u_A\gamma^\mu(c_LP_L+c_RP_R)u_X$ and
$\bar u_C\gamma^\mu(d_LP_L+d_RP_R)v_B$ for your declared helicity
configuration; the declared conventions fix them exactly (no free factor).
`mechanisms` states, for generic nonvanishing couplings, why each
configuration vanishes or not: the first bilinear (the $\bar\psi_A\ldots
\psi_X$ factor) vanishes, the second bilinear (the $\bar\psi_C\ldots\psi_B$
factor) vanishes, both are nonzero but the Lorentz contraction vanishes, or
the amplitude is nonzero.

### C2 certificate schema

Variables: `thB, thC, th, phi, cS, cA, dS, dA`.

```json
{
  "checkpoint": "C2",
  "amplitudes": {"<all 8 labels>": "<scalar expr>"},
  "separability_class": "<one of: fully_product | product_A_BC | product_B_AC | product_C_AB | GHZ_class | generalized_GHZ | W_class | generic_GTE>",
  "factors": {
    "single_party": "<A|B|C>",
    "single": ["<expr for |+> coeff>", "<expr for |-> coeff>"],
    "pair": {"++": "<expr>", "+-": "<expr>", "-+": "<expr>", "--": "<expr>"}
  },
  "entanglement": {"C_AB": "<expr>", "C_AC": "<expr>", "C_BC": "<expr>",
                   "C_A_BC": "<expr>", "C_B_AC": "<expr>", "C_C_AB": "<expr>",
                   "tau": "<expr>", "F3": "<expr>"},
  "bridge1": {
    "bipartition": "<A|BC or B|AC or C|AB>",
    "matrix": [["<expr>", "<expr>", "<expr>", "<expr>"],
               ["<expr>", "<expr>", "<expr>", "<expr>"]],
    "claimed_rank": "<integer: the rank you establish>"
  }
}
```

`separability_class` describes the exact structure of the normalized state
(`product_X_YZ` means party X factors from the entangled or unentangled pair
YZ; use `fully_product` if all three factor). `factors` is required only when
the class is `fully_product` or `product_*`: the reconstruction
`single ⊗ pair`, placed at the declared parties, must reproduce the amplitude
vector projectively. The pair keys are $(\lambda,\lambda')$ of the two
remaining parties in alphabetical order. `bridge1.matrix` is the coefficient
matrix of the declared bipartition, rows indexed by the single party's
$\lambda\in\{+,-\}$ (in this order) and columns by the pair labels
`++, +-, -+, --`; the verifier checks it projectively against the reference
amplitudes and verifies its numerical rank equals `claimed_rank`.
`entanglement` entries may be constants; they are compared numerically.

### C3 certificate schema

Variables for amplitudes: `thB, thC, th, phi, cM, cE, dM, dE`. Variables for
`entanglement` and `bridge2`: `m1, m2` — the components of the NORMALIZED
state on your declared `support`, in the declared order, i.e.
$|\Psi\rangle=m_1|s_1\rangle+m_2|s_2\rangle$.

```json
{
  "checkpoint": "C3",
  "amplitudes": {"<all 8 labels>": "<scalar expr>"},
  "classification": "<same vocabulary as C2>",
  "support": ["<label s1>", "<label s2>"],
  "entanglement": {"C_AB": "...", "C_AC": "...", "C_BC": "...",
                   "C_A_BC": "...", "C_B_AC": "...", "C_C_AB": "...",
                   "tau": "...", "F3": "..."},
  "bridge1": {"mechanisms": {"<all 8 labels>": "<same vocabulary as C1>"}},
  "bridge2": {"rho_party": "<A|B|C>",
              "rho_matrix": [["<expr>", "<expr>"], ["<expr>", "<expr>"]]}
}
```

`rho_matrix` is the reduced density matrix of the declared party in the
$\{|+\rangle,|-\rangle\}$ basis, as expressions in `m1, m2`; it is compared
entrywise against the reference.

### C4 certificate schema

Variables: `a, b, c, d` — the four nonzero complex coefficients of the
normalized vector-channel state, bound in the order of your declared
`support` list.

```json
{
  "checkpoint": "C4",
  "support": ["<label of a>", "<label of b>", "<label of c>", "<label of d>"],
  "entanglement": {"C_AB": "...", "C_AC": "...", "C_BC": "...",
                   "C_A_BC": "...", "C_B_AC": "...", "C_C_AB": "...",
                   "tau": "...", "F3": "..."},
  "bridge1": {"rho_pair": "<AB|AC|BC>",
              "rho_matrix": [[4x4 expressions]]},
  "bridge2": {"pair": "<same pair>",
              "sqrt_eigenvalues_desc": ["<expr>", "<expr>", "<expr>", "<expr>"]}
}
```

`rho_matrix` is the two-qubit reduced density matrix of the declared pair in
the basis `++, +-, -+, --` of that pair (parties in alphabetical order).
`sqrt_eigenvalues_desc` are the descending square roots $\sqrt{r_i}$ of the
eigenvalues of $\rho\widetilde\rho$ for the declared pair. Expressions are
evaluated at hidden random normalized $(a,b,c,d)$ and compared against a
direct reference computation on the corresponding state.

### C5 certificate schema

Array variables: `T` (the 3×3×3 correlation tensor), unit vectors
`B1, B2, C1, C2`. Array helpers are available. In `alice_max`, the names
`D1, D2` are bound to your own evaluated `D1, D2` vectors.

```json
{
  "checkpoint": "C5",
  "mermin":     {"D1": "<vector expr>", "D2": "<vector expr>", "alice_max": "<scalar expr in D1, D2>"},
  "svetlichny": {"D1": "<vector expr>", "D2": "<vector expr>", "alice_max": "<scalar expr in D1, D2>"}
}
```

Your `D1, D2` are compared (as an unordered pair, each up to overall sign)
against the reference Alice-coefficient vectors at hidden $(T,B_1,B_2,C_1,
C_2)$ probes, and your `alice_max` value must equal the reference maximum over
Alice's axes at the same probes.

### C6 certificate schema

Array variables: `T`, plus an orthonormal pair `Cp, Cm`. Array helpers are
available.

```json
{
  "checkpoint": "C6",
  "two_setting_axis": {"AB|C": <0|1|2>, "AC|B": <0|1|2>, "BC|A": <0|1|2>},
  "contracted_matrices": {"T_plus": "<matrix expr in T, Cp>",
                          "T_minus": "<matrix expr in T, Cm>"},
  "reduced_value": "<scalar expr in T, Cp, Cm>",
  "outer_maximization": "<one of: maximize_over_orthonormal_pair | fixed_pair_sufficient | maximize_over_C_plus_only | maximize_over_gamma_only | no_outer_search_needed>",
  "quantum_bound": <number>
}
```

`two_setting_axis` maps each assignment to the tensor index (0-based, in the
declared $(i,j,k)\leftrightarrow(A,B,C)$ order) that is contracted with the
two-setting observer's $C_\pm$ directions. `contracted_matrices` must
reproduce the reference contracted matrices (transposition convention
accepted if used consistently). `reduced_value` is the value of the
$B_{442}^{AB|C}$ objective after ALL analytic inner optimizations, as a
function of a FIXED orthonormal pair `(Cp, Cm)` — it is compared numerically
against the reference reduced objective at hidden $(T,C_+,C_-)$ probes.
`outer_maximization` must state what remains to be searched after the
reduction, and `quantum_bound` is the derived quantum upper bound of
$B_{442}$.

## Numerical solver requirements

Submit ONE self-contained Python file at `/app/outputs/solver.py` using only
the Python standard library, `numpy`, and optionally `scipy`. It must be
deterministic (fix all random seeds internally; repeated runs on the same
input must reproduce outputs to $10^{-9}$) and must implement three CLI modes:

```bash
python solver.py solve --input CASES.csv --output RESULTS.csv
python solver.py state --input CASES.csv --output STATES.json
python solver.py bell  --input REQUEST.json --output RESPONSE.json
```

- `solve`: for every input case, compute the normalized state and write one
  results row (schema below).
- `state`: for every input case, write the normalized 8-component state and
  the correlation tensor:
  `{"states": [{"case_id": "...", "psi_re_im": [[re, im] x 8], "T": [[[...]]] }]}`,
  with `psi_re_im` in the declared basis ordering and `T[i][j][k]` in the
  declared index order.
- `bell`: read `{"requests": [{"id": "...", "T": [[[...]]]}]}` — arbitrary
  physical 3×3×3 correlation tensors — and write
  `{"results": [{"id": "...", "B_M": x, "B_S": x, "B_442_AB_C": x,
  "B_442_AC_B": x, "B_442_BC_A": x, "B_442_sym": x}]}`.

The solver must genuinely compute its outputs from the input values. It must
not embed tables of precomputed results, must not branch on `case_id`, and
must not read any file other than the declared input. The verifier runs it on
fresh hidden cases, on perturbed variants of the public cases under public
identifiers, and on repeated inputs; confirmed lookup or input-ignoring
behavior caps the final score at 49.

Performance budget: the verifier's batches contain at most 12 cases per
`solve`/`state` call and at most 12 tensors per `bell` call. Budget roughly
2 minutes of compute per case (`solve`) and per tensor (`bell`); `state`
calls carry no Bell optimization and should be substantially faster. Small
batches receive proportionally smaller time slots (never less than ~2
minutes per item), and a full 12-item batch must finish well within 25
minutes on a standard 8-core container (the reference implementation needs
under one minute per full batch). Exceeding a batch's time slot forfeits
that batch's sub-tests.

## Input and output contracts

`CASES.csv` columns (exact order and names):

```text
case_id,interaction,theta_B,theta_C,theta,phi,c_S,c_A,d_S,d_A,c_L,c_R,d_L,d_R,c_M,c_E,d_M,d_E
```

`interaction` is one of `scalar`, `vector`, `tensor`; all couplings are real
floats and irrelevant couplings are zero; every evaluated row has a nonzero
total amplitude norm and lies in the nonsingular interior of phase space.

`RESULTS.csv` columns (exact order and names; all values finite reals,
at least 9 significant digits):

```text
case_id,C_AB,C_AC,C_BC,C_A_BC,C_B_AC,C_C_AB,tau,F3,B_M,B_S,B_442_AB_C,B_442_AC_B,B_442_BC_A,B_442_sym
```

All Bell columns are the nonnegative optimized absolute values defined above.

## Public smoke cases

Save the following three rows (with the header above) and run your solver on
them; write the resulting `RESULTS.csv` to `/app/outputs/results.csv`. These
rows exist for schema and sanity checking only — the graded numerical work
uses hidden cases supplied to your solver at verification time.

```csv
case_id,interaction,theta_B,theta_C,theta,phi,c_S,c_A,d_S,d_A,c_L,c_R,d_L,d_R,c_M,c_E,d_M,d_E
pub-1,scalar,1.85,2.10,0.65,0.85,0.9,-0.5,0.7,0.6,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0
pub-2,vector,2.05,1.75,1.15,-0.55,0,0,0,0,1.1,0.6,0.8,-0.9,0,0,0,0
pub-3,tensor,1.60,2.30,0.95,1.35,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0.85,0.45,-0.65,0.75
```

## Output files

Write all artifacts under `/app/outputs`:

- `/app/outputs/ANALYSIS.md`
- `/app/outputs/solver.py`
- `/app/outputs/results.csv`

## Output contract

Every file the hidden verifier reads is described below. Follow the schemas
exactly.

### ANALYSIS.md
- path: `/app/outputs/ANALYSIS.md`
- format: markdown with the fixed sections, marker blocks, and JSON
  certificates specified above
- purpose: scored (analytic checkpoints C1–C6)

### solver.py
- path: `/app/outputs/solver.py`
- format: single-file Python 3 program with the three CLI modes above
- purpose: scored (hidden numerical/generalization score)

### results.csv
- path: `/app/outputs/results.csv`
- format: csv with the exact RESULTS schema, one row per public smoke case
- purpose: output contract (schema, alignment, finiteness)

## Self-check before finishing (optional, not scored)

A machine-readable copy of the output contract is below. Before you finish,
verify: the three files exist; `ANALYSIS.md` contains all six checkpoint
sections with every marker pair appearing exactly once and each CERT block
holding exactly one parseable ```json fence; every FINAL and BRIDGE block
contains a display equation with an `=`; `results.csv` has the exact header
and three finite rows for `pub-1`, `pub-2`, `pub-3`; `python solver.py solve`
/ `state` / `bell` run cleanly on the public rows and a small tensor request.
This checks SHAPE ONLY — passing it does not mean the physics is correct.

```json
{
  "outputs": [
    {"file": "ANALYSIS.md", "format": "markdown",
     "required_markers": ["BRIDGE:Ci:1", "BRIDGE:Ci:2", "CHECKPOINT:Ci:FINAL",
                          "CHECKPOINT:Ci:CONSISTENCY", "CHECKPOINT:Ci:CERT"],
     "checkpoints": ["C1", "C2", "C3", "C4", "C5", "C6"]},
    {"file": "solver.py", "format": "python",
     "cli_modes": ["solve", "state", "bell"]},
    {"file": "results.csv", "format": "csv",
     "required_columns": ["case_id", "C_AB", "C_AC", "C_BC", "C_A_BC",
                          "C_B_AC", "C_C_AB", "tau", "F3", "B_M", "B_S",
                          "B_442_AB_C", "B_442_AC_B", "B_442_BC_A",
                          "B_442_sym"],
     "required_rows": ["pub-1", "pub-2", "pub-3"]}
  ]
}
```

## How you are scored

The hidden verifier computes a 0–100 score; `reward = score / 100`; the pass
line is 60.

- Analytic score D (70): binary checkpoints with weights C1=18, C2=6, C3=8,
  C4=10, C5=8, C6=20. Each checkpoint requires BOTH its final formula bundle
  (machine-checked through the certificates at hidden probe points, with the
  stated equivalence classes) AND all mandatory bridge artifacts (checked
  numerically and structurally) to be correct.
- Hidden numerical score N (25): complete hidden decay cases end-to-end (12),
  independent random three-qubit Bell-optimizer tests through the `bell` mode
  (8), phase/normalization/party-permutation invariance (3), optimizer
  determinism and boundary-near stability (2). Sub-tests accumulate; single
  failures cost only their sub-test.
- Output contract O (5): all-or-nothing mechanical check of the three
  artifacts.

Score caps, all applied simultaneously (final = min of raw score and every
applicable cap): missing/empty/unrecognizable ANALYSIS.md → 39; missing or
unrunnable solver, or confirmed lookup/hardcoding → 49; C1 failed or C6
failed → 59; fewer than 4 checkpoints passed → 59; N < 15 → 59; O = 0 → 59.

Numerical comparison bounds (absolute unless stated): optimized Bell values
1e-3 (2e-3 for permutation-invariance consistency, 5e-3 for the
near-degenerate stability probe); entanglement quantities 5e-7 (F3 2e-6);
correlation-tensor entries 1e-7; states and amplitude vectors by projective
fidelity 1 − F ≤ 1e-9; certificate bridge artifacts 1e-6 relative to scale;
amplitude components are treated as zero below 1e-8 of the vector's largest
component; determinism repeats must agree to 1e-9. Tolerances were
calibrated so that a correct implementation passes with orders-of-magnitude
margin; they are far below the error scale of any wrong formula or missing
optimization.

topicContent:
# From Four-Fermion Decay Operators to Tripartite Bell Nonlocality

## Problem background

A massive spin-1/2 fermion $X$ decays at rest into three massless fermions,
$X\to A+B+C$, where $A$ and $C$ are outgoing fermions and $B$ is an outgoing
antifermion. At a fixed phase-space point the decay produces a pure three-qubit
state in the helicity basis of the three final particles. The structure of that
state — and therefore its multipartite entanglement and its ability to violate
tripartite Bell inequalities — is controlled by the Lorentz structure of the
four-fermion contact interaction driving the decay.

This is a closed-book analytic–numerical task. Everything needed to define the
targets is stated below; no external literature is required or permitted as a
source of final formulas. You must derive six load-bearing analytic results,
implement a general numerical solver, and package both according to the exact
output contract in this document.

> **Closed-book rule (binding).** Work only from this document and your own
> reasoning and computation. Do NOT access the network for any purpose: do not
> search the web, do not download or fetch papers, preprints, datasets, or
> code, and do not call any external API or model. Do not use `curl`, `wget`,
> `pip install` from remote indexes, `git clone`, or any browser/search tool.
> All derivations must be your own; all required numerical libraries (numpy,
> and optionally scipy) are already available in the environment. Retrieving
> the source paper, a published result, or any external solution is a
> disqualifying violation of the task.

## Scientific objective

For scalar, vector, and tensor four-fermion interactions:

1. derive the helicity amplitudes and the normalized three-qubit helicity
   state at an arbitrary phase-space point;
2. derive the entanglement structure (pairwise concurrences, one-to-rest
   concurrences, three-tangle $\tau$, and the concurrence-triangle measure
   $F_3$);
3. analytically reduce and then numerically optimize the Mermin, Svetlichny,
   and tight $4\times4\times2$ Bell observables;
4. implement a general solver that evaluates all of these quantities for
   hidden kinematic and coupling configurations supplied at verification time.

Your submission must not rely on hard-coded rows, memorized output tables, or
branching on case identifiers. The verifier runs your solver on fresh hidden
inputs and rejects confirmed lookup behavior.

## Kinematics

Work in the rest frame of $X$: $p_X^\mu=(m,0,0,0)$. Set $m=1$ in numerical
work. The decay plane is the $x$–$z$ plane:

$$
p_A^\mu=p_A(1,0,0,1),\qquad
p_B^\mu=p_B(1,\sin\theta_B,0,\cos\theta_B),\qquad
p_C^\mu=p_C(1,-\sin\theta_C,0,\cos\theta_C).
$$

Energy–momentum conservation fixes

$$
p_A=-mD\sin(\theta_B+\theta_C),\qquad
p_B=mD\sin\theta_C,\qquad
p_C=mD\sin\theta_B,\qquad
D=\frac{1}{\sin\theta_B+\sin\theta_C-\sin(\theta_B+\theta_C)} .
$$

All evaluated configurations lie in the nonsingular physical interior

$$
0<\theta_B,\theta_C<\pi,\qquad \pi<\theta_B+\theta_C<2\pi .
$$

The initial spin-polarization direction of $X$ is
$\boldsymbol n=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ \sin\theta\sin\phi,\ \cos\theta)$.

## Dirac and spinor conventions

These conventions are binding; every convention-sensitive choice below is part
of the target definition. Use

$$
g_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1),\qquad
\epsilon^{0123}=+1,\qquad \epsilon_{0123}=-1 .
$$

Dirac representation:

$$
\gamma^0=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf 1_2&0\\0&-\mathbf 1_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\gamma^i=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_i\\-\sigma_i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\gamma^5=i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3,
$$

$$
P_L=\frac{1-\gamma^5}{2},\qquad P_R=\frac{1+\gamma^5}{2},\qquad
\sigma^{\mu\nu}=\frac{i}{2}[\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu],\qquad
\sigma_{\mu\nu}=g_{\mu\alpha}g_{\nu\beta}\sigma^{\alpha\beta} .
$$

Repeated Lorentz indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.

For a momentum direction
$\widehat{\boldsymbol p}=(\sin\vartheta\cos\varphi_p,\
\sin\vartheta\sin\varphi_p,\ \cos\vartheta)$ define the helicity two-spinors

$$
\chi_+(\vartheta,\varphi_p)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\vartheta/2)\\
e^{i\varphi_p}\sin(\vartheta/2)\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\chi_-(\vartheta,\varphi_p)=\begin{pmatrix}-e^{-i\varphi_p}\sin(\vartheta/2)\\
\cos(\vartheta/2)\end{pmatrix},
$$

so that $(\widehat{\boldsymbol p}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)\chi_\lambda
=\lambda\chi_\lambda$ with $\lambda=\pm1$. Use the massless spinors

$$
u(p,\lambda)=\sqrt E\begin{pmatrix}\chi_\lambda\\ \lambda\chi_\lambda
\end{pmatrix},\qquad
v(p,\lambda)=\sqrt E\begin{pmatrix}\chi_{-\lambda}\\ -\lambda\chi_{-\lambda}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Particle $B$ is the outgoing antifermion and is represented by
$v_B(p_B,\lambda_B)$. The incoming polarized rest-frame spinor is

$$
u_X(\boldsymbol n)=\sqrt{2m}\,
\big(\cos(\theta/2),\ e^{i\phi}\sin(\theta/2),\ 0,\ 0\big)^T ,
$$

and $\bar u=u^\dagger\gamma^0$, $\bar v=v^\dagger\gamma^0$. For the three
outgoing momenta use the literal direction angles

$$
(\vartheta_A,\varphi_A)=(0,0),\qquad
(\vartheta_B,\varphi_B)=(\theta_B,0),\qquad
(\vartheta_C,\varphi_C)=(\theta_C,\pi).
$$

Use these azimuths as literal constants; do not reconstruct them from momentum
components.

## Four-fermion interactions

All couplings are real numbers.

Scalar:

$$
\mathcal O_S=\left[\bar\psi_A(c_S+ic_A\gamma^5)\psi_X\right]
\left[\bar\psi_C(d_S+id_A\gamma^5)\psi_B\right].
$$

Vector:

$$
\mathcal O_V=\left[\bar\psi_A\gamma_\mu(c_LP_L+c_RP_R)\psi_X\right]
\left[\bar\psi_C\gamma^\mu(d_LP_L+d_RP_R)\psi_B\right].
$$

Tensor:

$$
\mathcal O_T=\left[\bar\psi_A(c_M+ic_E\gamma^5)\sigma^{\mu\nu}\psi_X\right]
\left[\bar\psi_C(d_M+id_E\gamma^5)\sigma_{\mu\nu}\psi_B\right].
$$

Any overall EFT coefficient common to all helicity amplitudes of one
interaction cancels after normalization and may be dropped.

## Helicity state and basis ordering

For interaction $I\in\{S,V,T\}$ compute
$\mathcal M^I_{\lambda_A\lambda_B\lambda_C}$ directly from the spinor
contractions and construct

$$
|\Psi_I\rangle=\frac{1}{\mathcal N_I}
\sum_{\lambda_A\lambda_B\lambda_C}
\mathcal M^I_{\lambda_A\lambda_B\lambda_C}
|\lambda_A\lambda_B\lambda_C\rangle,
\qquad
\mathcal N_I^2=\sum_{\lambda_A\lambda_B\lambda_C}
\big|\mathcal M^I_{\lambda_A\lambda_B\lambda_C}\big|^2 .
$$

Identify $|+\rangle\equiv|0\rangle$ and $|-\rangle\equiv|1\rangle$. The
eight-dimensional ordering is

$$
|{+}{+}{+}\rangle,\ |{+}{+}{-}\rangle,\ |{+}{-}{+}\rangle,\ |{+}{-}{-}\rangle,\
|{-}{+}{+}\rangle,\ |{-}{+}{-}\rangle,\ |{-}{-}{+}\rangle,\ |{-}{-}{-}\rangle ,
$$

i.e. component index $=4b(\lambda_A)+2b(\lambda_B)+b(\lambda_C)$ with
$b(+)=0$, $b(-)=1$. Two unnormalized amplitude vectors differing by one common
nonzero complex factor are physically equivalent; a normalized state is defined
up to a global phase.

## Quantum-information definitions

Pauli matrices in the declared computational basis:

$$
\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For $\rho=|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|$ define the correlation tensor

$$
T_{ijk}=\operatorname{Tr}\big[\rho\,\sigma_i\otimes\sigma_j\otimes\sigma_k\big],
\qquad i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\},
$$

with subsystem index order $(i,j,k)\leftrightarrow(A,B,C)$.

Two-qubit concurrence of a reduced state $\rho_{IJ}$: with
$\widetilde\rho_{IJ}=(\sigma_2\otimes\sigma_2)\rho_{IJ}^*
(\sigma_2\otimes\sigma_2)$ (conjugation in the declared basis) and
$r_1\ge r_2\ge r_3\ge r_4\ge0$ the eigenvalues of
$\rho_{IJ}\widetilde\rho_{IJ}$ (tiny negative roundoff clipped),

$$
C_{IJ}=\max\big(0,\ \sqrt{r_1}-\sqrt{r_2}-\sqrt{r_3}-\sqrt{r_4}\big).
$$

One-to-rest concurrence of the pure three-qubit state:

$$
C_{A(BC)}=\sqrt{2\big(1-\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^2\big)},\qquad
\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_{BC}\,\rho ,
$$

and cyclically for $C_{B(AC)}$, $C_{C(AB)}$. Three-tangle:

$$
\tau=C_{A(BC)}^2-C_{AB}^2-C_{AC}^2 ,
$$

with values in $[-10^{-12},0]$ clipped to zero. Concurrence-triangle measure:

$$
Q=\frac{C_{A(BC)}+C_{B(AC)}+C_{C(AB)}}{2},\qquad
F_3=\frac{4}{\sqrt3}\sqrt{Q\big(Q-C_{A(BC)}\big)\big(Q-C_{B(AC)}\big)
\big(Q-C_{C(AB)}\big)} ,
$$

with a radicand in $[-10^{-12},0]$ clipped to zero.

## Bell observables

For a real unit vector $\boldsymbol a$ write $A_r=\boldsymbol
A_r\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$, and similarly $B_s$, $C_t$. Every reported Bell
value is the maximum of the absolute expectation value over all measurement
axes.

Mermin:

$$
\mathcal B_M=A_1B_1C_2+A_1B_2C_1+A_2B_1C_1-A_2B_2C_2,\qquad
B_M^{\max}(\rho)=\max\big|\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\,\mathcal B_M)\big| ,
$$

with bounds $B_M^{\rm FLR}\le2$ (fully local) and $B_M^{\rm QM}\le4$.

Svetlichny:

$$
\mathcal B_S=A_1B_1C_1+A_1B_1C_2+A_1B_2C_1+A_2B_1C_1
-A_2B_2C_2-A_2B_2C_1-A_2B_1C_2-A_1B_2C_2 ,
$$

with bounds $B_S^{\rm BLR}\le4$ (biseparable) and $B_S^{\rm QM}\le4\sqrt2$.

Tight $4\times4\times2$ operator, for four settings on the first two listed
parties and two settings on the third:

$$
\mathcal B_{442}^{AB|C}
=\big[A_1(B_1+B_2)+A_2(B_1-B_2)\big](C_1+C_2)
+\big[A_3(B_3+B_4)+A_4(B_3-B_4)\big](C_1-C_2).
$$

Define the optimized values $B_{442}^{AB|C}$, $B_{442}^{AC|B}$,
$B_{442}^{BC|A}$ by the corresponding particle assignments (the party after
the bar is the two-setting observer; assignments must be implemented by
consistent permutation of the tensor indices, not by independent formulas),
and

$$
B_{442}^{\rm sym}=\max\big(B_{442}^{AB|C},B_{442}^{AC|B},B_{442}^{BC|A}\big),
$$

with bounds $B_{442}^{\rm FLR}\le4$ and $B_{442}^{\rm QM}\le8$.

## Analytic checkpoints

Six checkpoints are scored, each binary: a checkpoint earns credit only when
its complete final formula bundle is correct AND all of its mandatory bridge
obligations are present, valid, and non-circular. Partial correctness within a
checkpoint earns nothing. C1 and C6 are mandatory load-bearing checkpoints:
failing either caps the final score at 59.

### C1. Vector helicity amplitudes (mandatory)

Starting from $\mathcal O_V$: derive all nonzero helicity amplitudes; prove
that all other helicity configurations vanish in the massless limit; give the
resulting unnormalized four-component amplitude vector up to one common
nonzero complex factor; construct the normalized state in the declared
eight-dimensional ordering.

Mandatory bridges: (1) explicitly evaluate at least one nonzero product of
spinor currents; (2) use chiral projectors and the massless helicity structure
to justify the complete vanishing set.

### C2. Scalar-channel structure

Starting from $\mathcal O_S$: derive all nonzero helicity amplitudes;
determine the separability class; derive an explicit tensor-product
representation if one exists; derive the pairwise concurrences, one-to-rest
concurrences, $\tau$, and $F_3$.

Mandatory bridges: (1) write a coefficient matrix across a relevant
bipartition; (2) establish factorization or non-factorization by an explicit
rank, determinant, or equivalent Schmidt argument.

### C3. Tensor-channel structure

Starting from $\mathcal O_T$: derive all nonzero helicity amplitudes; classify
the state; derive the pairwise and one-to-rest concurrences; derive $\tau$ and
$F_3$.

Mandatory bridges: (1) explain the helicity selection that removes the other
six basis states; (2) explicitly compute at least one single-qubit reduced
density matrix.

### C4. Entanglement of the generic vector state

Write the normalized vector-channel state in terms of its four nonzero complex
coefficients and derive closed forms for $C_{AB}$, $C_{AC}$, $C_{BC}$,
$C_{A(BC)}$, $C_{B(AC)}$, $C_{C(AB)}$, $\tau$, and $F_3$.

Mandatory bridges: (1) explicitly calculate at least one two-qubit reduced
density matrix; (2) explicitly apply the Wootters construction or the CKW
relation — merely naming it is insufficient.

### C5. Partial analytic optimization of Mermin and Svetlichny

Starting from the explicit Bell operators and $T_{ijk}$: isolate Alice's two
measurement vectors; maximize analytically over them; reduce each problem to a
numerical optimization over Bob's and Charlie's four unit vectors.

Mandatory bridges: (1) explicitly derive the two three-vectors multiplying
Alice's axes; (2) justify the maximization via the maximum of a linear
functional on the unit sphere.

### C6. Semi-analytic optimization of B_442 (mandatory)

Starting from the ten-axis definition: introduce normalized sum/difference
vectors; analytically optimize all variables except one orthonormal pair;
reduce the outer search to three angular variables; derive the eigenvalue
expression; retain the outer maximization over the orthonormal pair; derive
the quantum upper bound 8.

Mandatory bridges: (1) correctly construct the two contracted $3\times3$
matrices associated with the two orthogonal directions of the two-setting
observer; (2) explicitly use Rayleigh–Ritz or an equivalent eigenvalue
variational argument to obtain the two largest eigenvalues.

## ANALYSIS.md requirements

Write your derivations to `/app/outputs/ANALYSIS.md` with EXACTLY the
following six top-level sections, in order, with these titles:

```markdown
# C1 Vector helicity amplitudes
# C2 Scalar-channel structure
# C3 Tensor-channel structure
# C4 Entanglement of the generic vector state
# C5 Partial analytic optimization of Mermin and Svetlichny
# C6 Semi-analytic optimization of B_442
```

Each section must contain the subsections `## Starting point`,
`## Mandatory bridge 1`, `## Mandatory bridge 2`, `## Final derived formula`,
`## Consistency check`, and `## Machine-readable certificate`, and the
following marker blocks (shown for C1; use the matching checkpoint id):

- `<!-- BRIDGE:C1:1:BEGIN -->` … `<!-- BRIDGE:C1:1:END -->` around bridge 1;
- `<!-- BRIDGE:C1:2:BEGIN -->` … `<!-- BRIDGE:C1:2:END -->` around bridge 2;
- `<!-- CHECKPOINT:C1:FINAL:BEGIN -->` … `<!-- CHECKPOINT:C1:FINAL:END -->`
  around the final formula bundle;
- `<!-- CHECKPOINT:C1:CONSISTENCY:BEGIN -->` …
  `<!-- CHECKPOINT:C1:CONSISTENCY:END -->` around the consistency check;
- `<!-- CHECKPOINT:C1:CERT:BEGIN -->` … `<!-- CHECKPOINT:C1:CERT:END -->`
  around one fenced ```json code block holding the machine-readable
  certificate.

Formal requirements, enforced mechanically:

1. Each marker pair must appear exactly once; duplicated or unbalanced markers
   invalidate the checkpoint.
2. Formulas must be text/LaTeX, never images. Every FINAL block and every
   BRIDGE block must contain at least one display equation
   (`$$ … $$` or `\[ … \]`) containing an `=` sign, with real mathematical
   content — bridges must show actual equations or algebraic transformations,
   not keywords.
3. The final formula of a checkpoint may not be assumed as its starting point;
   bridge blocks must contain the intermediate objects listed in the
   certificate schemas below.
4. Each consistency check must apply at least one of: normalization, symmetry,
   separable limit, GHZ limit, Bell bound, or direct substitution, and must
   include one fenced ```json block of the form
   `{"type": "<one of: normalization|symmetry|separable_limit|ghz_limit|bell_bound|direct_substitution>", "lhs": <number>, "rhs": <number>}`
   whose two numbers agree to within $10^{-6}$ (relative or absolute).
5. `ANALYSIS.md` must not exceed 5 MB.

## Machine-readable certificates

Because grading is deterministic, each checkpoint's final formulas and bridge
artifacts must also be supplied as machine-checkable expressions inside the
CERT block. The verifier evaluates your expressions at hidden generic points
and compares them with an independent reference implementation. Expressions
that fail to parse, reference undeclared names, or error/overflow at any valid
probe point score zero for that checkpoint.

### Expression language

Expressions are single-line Python-syntax strings. Allowed: numbers, the
declared variable names, parentheses, `+ - * / **`, whitespace, and calls to
the allowed functions. Character set: letters, digits, `_ + - * / ( ) , .`
and whitespace (space or tab). No indexing/brackets, no attribute access, no
double underscores, no strings. Maximum 4096 characters per expression.

Scalar functions: `sin`, `cos`, `exp`, `sqrt`, `conjugate`, `Abs`; constants
`I` (imaginary unit) and `pi`. All arithmetic is complex; `sqrt` is the
principal complex square root; `Abs` returns a real number.

In addition to the per-checkpoint variables listed below, the convention
constant `m` (bound to $1$) and the on-shell momentum magnitudes `pA`, `pB`,
`pC` (the $p_A,p_B,p_C$ of the kinematics section, functions of
$\theta_B,\theta_C$) are bound in every certificate expression. You may write
amplitude expressions either in reduced form (angles/couplings only) or with
explicit mass/momentum factors; amplitude vectors are compared projectively,
so any overall factor cancels.

Array helpers (available only where stated): for a rank-$n$ array `X`, a
3-vector `v`, and 3×3 matrices `M`, `N`:

- `contract(X, v, axis)`: contract index `axis` (0-based) of `X` with `v`;
  e.g. `contract(T, v, 2)` is the 3×3 matrix $\sum_k T_{ijk}v_k$, and
  `contract(M, v, 1)` is the 3-vector $\sum_j M_{ij}v_j$.
- `matmul(M, N)`: matrix product; `transpose(M)`: matrix transpose.
- `norm(v)`: Euclidean norm; `dot(u, v)`: real dot product;
  `cross(u, v)`: cross product.
- `sum_top_eigs(M, k)`: sum of the `k` largest eigenvalues of the symmetric
  matrix `M` (the argument must be symmetric to $10^{-9}$).
- `sqrt`, `Abs` also apply to real scalars in this context.

Neutral worked example (no relation to this task): a certificate field for a
point-charge field magnitude could be `"E": "q/(4*pi*eps*r**2)"`; a vector
certificate built from a matrix `M` and vector `v` could be
`"w": "contract(M, v, 1)"`, meaning $w_i=\sum_j M_{ij}v_j$.

### Helicity labels

Helicity configurations are three-character strings over `+`/`-` in the order
$(\lambda_A,\lambda_B,\lambda_C)$, e.g. `"+-+"` means $\lambda_A=+1,
\lambda_B=-1,\lambda_C=+1$.

### C1 certificate schema

Variables: `thB, thC, th, phi, cL, cR, dL, dR` (angles in radians), plus the
always-bound `m, pA, pB, pC` described above (the bridge-1 spinor-current
components are naturally written with these momentum factors).

```json
{
  "checkpoint": "C1",
  "amplitudes": {"<all 8 helicity labels>": "<scalar expr; write 0 for vanishing components>"},
  "bridge1": {
    "helicity": "<one label with nonzero amplitude at generic couplings>",
    "current_AX": ["<expr mu=0>", "<expr mu=1>", "<expr mu=2>", "<expr mu=3>"],
    "current_CB": ["<expr mu=0>", "<expr mu=1>", "<expr mu=2>", "<expr mu=3>"]
  },
  "bridge2": {
    "mechanisms": {"<all 8 labels>": "<one of: nonzero | first_bilinear_vanishes | second_bilinear_vanishes | lorentz_contraction_vanishes>"}
  }
}
```

`amplitudes` is graded per hidden point by projective fidelity of the full
8-component vector against the reference (one common complex factor allowed),
plus exact agreement of the zero set. `current_AX` and `current_CB` are the
contravariant components of $\bar u_A\gamma^\mu(c_LP_L+c_RP_R)u_X$ and
$\bar u_C\gamma^\mu(d_LP_L+d_RP_R)v_B$ for your declared helicity
configuration; the declared conventions fix them exactly (no free factor).
`mechanisms` states, for generic nonvanishing couplings, why each
configuration vanishes or not: the first bilinear (the $\bar\psi_A\ldots
\psi_X$ factor) vanishes, the second bilinear (the $\bar\psi_C\ldots\psi_B$
factor) vanishes, both are nonzero but the Lorentz contraction vanishes, or
the amplitude is nonzero.

### C2 certificate schema

Variables: `thB, thC, th, phi, cS, cA, dS, dA`.

```json
{
  "checkpoint": "C2",
  "amplitudes": {"<all 8 labels>": "<scalar expr>"},
  "separability_class": "<one of: fully_product | product_A_BC | product_B_AC | product_C_AB | GHZ_class | generalized_GHZ | W_class | generic_GTE>",
  "factors": {
    "single_party": "<A|B|C>",
    "single": ["<expr for |+> coeff>", "<expr for |-> coeff>"],
    "pair": {"++": "<expr>", "+-": "<expr>", "-+": "<expr>", "--": "<expr>"}
  },
  "entanglement": {"C_AB": "<expr>", "C_AC": "<expr>", "C_BC": "<expr>",
                   "C_A_BC": "<expr>", "C_B_AC": "<expr>", "C_C_AB": "<expr>",
                   "tau": "<expr>", "F3": "<expr>"},
  "bridge1": {
    "bipartition": "<A|BC or B|AC or C|AB>",
    "matrix": [["<expr>", "<expr>", "<expr>", "<expr>"],
               ["<expr>", "<expr>", "<expr>", "<expr>"]],
    "claimed_rank": "<integer: the rank you establish>"
  }
}
```

`separability_class` describes the exact structure of the normalized state
(`product_X_YZ` means party X factors from the entangled or unentangled pair
YZ; use `fully_product` if all three factor). `factors` is required only when
the class is `fully_product` or `product_*`: the reconstruction
`single ⊗ pair`, placed at the declared parties, must reproduce the amplitude
vector projectively. The pair keys are $(\lambda,\lambda')$ of the two
remaining parties in alphabetical order. `bridge1.matrix` is the coefficient
matrix of the declared bipartition, rows indexed by the single party's
$\lambda\in\{+,-\}$ (in this order) and columns by the pair labels
`++, +-, -+, --`; the verifier checks it projectively against the reference
amplitudes and verifies its numerical rank equals `claimed_rank`.
`entanglement` entries may be constants; they are compared numerically.

### C3 certificate schema

Variables for amplitudes: `thB, thC, th, phi, cM, cE, dM, dE`. Variables for
`entanglement` and `bridge2`: `m1, m2` — the components of the NORMALIZED
state on your declared `support`, in the declared order, i.e.
$|\Psi\rangle=m_1|s_1\rangle+m_2|s_2\rangle$.

```json
{
  "checkpoint": "C3",
  "amplitudes": {"<all 8 labels>": "<scalar expr>"},
  "classification": "<same vocabulary as C2>",
  "support": ["<label s1>", "<label s2>"],
  "entanglement": {"C_AB": "...", "C_AC": "...", "C_BC": "...",
                   "C_A_BC": "...", "C_B_AC": "...", "C_C_AB": "...",
                   "tau": "...", "F3": "..."},
  "bridge1": {"mechanisms": {"<all 8 labels>": "<same vocabulary as C1>"}},
  "bridge2": {"rho_party": "<A|B|C>",
              "rho_matrix": [["<expr>", "<expr>"], ["<expr>", "<expr>"]]}
}
```

`rho_matrix` is the reduced density matrix of the declared party in the
$\{|+\rangle,|-\rangle\}$ basis, as expressions in `m1, m2`; it is compared
entrywise against the reference.

### C4 certificate schema

Variables: `a, b, c, d` — the four nonzero complex coefficients of the
normalized vector-channel state, bound in the order of your declared
`support` list.

```json
{
  "checkpoint": "C4",
  "support": ["<label of a>", "<label of b>", "<label of c>", "<label of d>"],
  "entanglement": {"C_AB": "...", "C_AC": "...", "C_BC": "...",
                   "C_A_BC": "...", "C_B_AC": "...", "C_C_AB": "...",
                   "tau": "...", "F3": "..."},
  "bridge1": {"rho_pair": "<AB|AC|BC>",
              "rho_matrix": [[4x4 expressions]]},
  "bridge2": {"pair": "<same pair>",
              "sqrt_eigenvalues_desc": ["<expr>", "<expr>", "<expr>", "<expr>"]}
}
```

`rho_matrix` is the two-qubit reduced density matrix of the declared pair in
the basis `++, +-, -+, --` of that pair (parties in alphabetical order).
`sqrt_eigenvalues_desc` are the descending square roots $\sqrt{r_i}$ of the
eigenvalues of $\rho\widetilde\rho$ for the declared pair. Expressions are
evaluated at hidden random normalized $(a,b,c,d)$ and compared against a
direct reference computation on the corresponding state.

### C5 certificate schema

Array variables: `T` (the 3×3×3 correlation tensor), unit vectors
`B1, B2, C1, C2`. Array helpers are available. In `alice_max`, the names
`D1, D2` are bound to your own evaluated `D1, D2` vectors.

```json
{
  "checkpoint": "C5",
  "mermin":     {"D1": "<vector expr>", "D2": "<vector expr>", "alice_max": "<scalar expr in D1, D2>"},
  "svetlichny": {"D1": "<vector expr>", "D2": "<vector expr>", "alice_max": "<scalar expr in D1, D2>"}
}
```

Your `D1, D2` are compared (as an unordered pair, each up to overall sign)
against the reference Alice-coefficient vectors at hidden $(T,B_1,B_2,C_1,
C_2)$ probes, and your `alice_max` value must equal the reference maximum over
Alice's axes at the same probes.

### C6 certificate schema

Array variables: `T`, plus an orthonormal pair `Cp, Cm`. Array helpers are
available.

```json
{
  "checkpoint": "C6",
  "two_setting_axis": {"AB|C": <0|1|2>, "AC|B": <0|1|2>, "BC|A": <0|1|2>},
  "contracted_matrices": {"T_plus": "<matrix expr in T, Cp>",
                          "T_minus": "<matrix expr in T, Cm>"},
  "reduced_value": "<scalar expr in T, Cp, Cm>",
  "outer_maximization": "<one of: maximize_over_orthonormal_pair | fixed_pair_sufficient | maximize_over_C_plus_only | maximize_over_gamma_only | no_outer_search_needed>",
  "quantum_bound": <number>
}
```

`two_setting_axis` maps each assignment to the tensor index (0-based, in the
declared $(i,j,k)\leftrightarrow(A,B,C)$ order) that is contracted with the
two-setting observer's $C_\pm$ directions. `contracted_matrices` must
reproduce the reference contracted matrices (transposition convention
accepted if used consistently). `reduced_value` is the value of the
$B_{442}^{AB|C}$ objective after ALL analytic inner optimizations, as a
function of a FIXED orthonormal pair `(Cp, Cm)` — it is compared numerically
against the reference reduced objective at hidden $(T,C_+,C_-)$ probes.
`outer_maximization` must state what remains to be searched after the
reduction, and `quantum_bound` is the derived quantum upper bound of
$B_{442}$.

## Numerical solver requirements

Submit ONE self-contained Python file at `/app/outputs/solver.py` using only
the Python standard library, `numpy`, and optionally `scipy`. It must be
deterministic (fix all random seeds internally; repeated runs on the same
input must reproduce outputs to $10^{-9}$) and must implement three CLI modes:

```bash
python solver.py solve --input CASES.csv --output RESULTS.csv
python solver.py state --input CASES.csv --output STATES.json
python solver.py bell  --input REQUEST.json --output RESPONSE.json
```

- `solve`: for every input case, compute the normalized state and write one
  results row (schema below).
- `state`: for every input case, write the normalized 8-component state and
  the correlation tensor:
  `{"states": [{"case_id": "...", "psi_re_im": [[re, im] x 8], "T": [[[...]]] }]}`,
  with `psi_re_im` in the declared basis ordering and `T[i][j][k]` in the
  declared index order.
- `bell`: read `{"requests": [{"id": "...", "T": [[[...]]]}]}` — arbitrary
  physical 3×3×3 correlation tensors — and write
  `{"results": [{"id": "...", "B_M": x, "B_S": x, "B_442_AB_C": x,
  "B_442_AC_B": x, "B_442_BC_A": x, "B_442_sym": x}]}`.

The solver must genuinely compute its outputs from the input values. It must
not embed tables of precomputed results, must not branch on `case_id`, and
must not read any file other than the declared input. The verifier runs it on
fresh hidden cases, on perturbed variants of the public cases under public
identifiers, and on repeated inputs; confirmed lookup or input-ignoring
behavior caps the final score at 49.

Performance budget: the verifier's batches contain at most 12 cases per
`solve`/`state` call and at most 12 tensors per `bell` call. Budget roughly
2 minutes of compute per case (`solve`) and per tensor (`bell`); `state`
calls carry no Bell optimization and should be substantially faster. Small
batches receive proportionally smaller time slots (never less than ~2
minutes per item), and a full 12-item batch must finish well within 25
minutes on a standard 8-core container (the reference implementation needs
under one minute per full batch). Exceeding a batch's time slot forfeits
that batch's sub-tests.

## Input and output contracts

`CASES.csv` columns (exact order and names):

```text
case_id,interaction,theta_B,theta_C,theta,phi,c_S,c_A,d_S,d_A,c_L,c_R,d_L,d_R,c_M,c_E,d_M,d_E
```

`interaction` is one of `scalar`, `vector`, `tensor`; all couplings are real
floats and irrelevant couplings are zero; every evaluated row has a nonzero
total amplitude norm and lies in the nonsingular interior of phase space.

`RESULTS.csv` columns (exact order and names; all values finite reals,
at least 9 significant digits):

```text
case_id,C_AB,C_AC,C_BC,C_A_BC,C_B_AC,C_C_AB,tau,F3,B_M,B_S,B_442_AB_C,B_442_AC_B,B_442_BC_A,B_442_sym
```

All Bell columns are the nonnegative optimized absolute values defined above.

## Public smoke cases

Save the following three rows (with the header above) and run your solver on
them; write the resulting `RESULTS.csv` to `/app/outputs/results.csv`. These
rows exist for schema and sanity checking only — the graded numerical work
uses hidden cases supplied to your solver at verification time.

```csv

pub-1,scalar,1.85,2.10,0.65,0.85,0.9,-0.5,0.7,0.6,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0
pub-2,vector,2.05,1.75,1.15,-0.55,0,0,0,0,1.1,0.6,0.8,-0.9,0,0,0,0
pub-3,tensor,1.60,2.30,0.95,1.35,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0.85,0.45,-0.65,0.75
```

## Output files

Write all artifacts under `/app/outputs`:

- `/app/outputs/ANALYSIS.md`
- `/app/outputs/solver.py`
- `/app/outputs/results.csv`

## Output contract

Every file the hidden verifier reads is described below. Follow the schemas
exactly.

### ANALYSIS.md
- path: `/app/outputs/ANALYSIS.md`
- format: markdown with the fixed sections, marker blocks, and JSON
  certificates specified above
- purpose: scored (analytic checkpoints C1–C6)

### solver.py
- path: `/app/outputs/solver.py`
- format: single-file Python 3 program with the three CLI modes above
- purpose: scored (hidden numerical/generalization score)

### results.csv
- path: `/app/outputs/results.csv`
- format: csv with the exact RESULTS schema, one row per public smoke case

## Self-check before finishing (optional, not scored)

A machine-readable copy of the output contract is below. Before you finish,
verify: the three files exist; `ANALYSIS.md` contains all six checkpoint
sections with every marker pair appearing exactly once and each CERT block
holding exactly one parseable ```json fence; every FINAL and BRIDGE block
contains a display equation with an `=`; `results.csv` has the exact header
and three finite rows for `pub-1`, `pub-2`, `pub-3`; `python solver.py solve`
/ `state` / `bell` run cleanly on the public rows and a small tensor request.
This checks SHAPE ONLY — passing it does not mean the physics is correct.

```json
{
  "outputs": [
    {"file": "ANALYSIS.md", "format": "markdown",
     "required_markers": ["BRIDGE:Ci:1", "BRIDGE:Ci:2", "CHECKPOINT:Ci:FINAL",
                          "CHECKPOINT:Ci:CONSISTENCY", "CHECKPOINT:Ci:CERT"],
     "checkpoints": ["C1", "C2", "C3", "C4", "C5", "C6"]},
    {"file": "solver.py", "format": "python",
     "cli_modes": ["solve", "state", "bell"]},
    {"file": "results.csv", "format": "csv",
     "required_columns": ["case_id", "C_AB", "C_AC", "C_BC", "C_A_BC",
                          "C_B_AC", "C_C_AB", "tau", "F3", "B_M", "B_S",
                          "B_442_AB_C", "B_442_AC_B", "B_442_BC_A",
                          "B_442_sym"],
     "required_rows": ["pub-1", "pub-2", "pub-3"]}
  ]
}
```

## How you are scored

The hidden verifier computes a 0–100 score; `reward = score / 100`; the pass
line is 60.

- Analytic score D (70): binary checkpoints with weights C1=18, C2=6, C3=8,
  C4=10, C5=8, C6=20. Each checkpoint requires BOTH its final formula bundle
  (machine-checked through the certificates at hidden probe points, with the
  stated equivalence classes) AND all mandatory bridge artifacts (checked
  numerically and structurally) to be correct.
- Hidden numerical score N (25): complete hidden decay cases end-to-end (12),
  independent random three-qubit Bell-optimizer tests through the `bell` mode
  (8), phase/normalization/party-permutation invariance (3), optimizer
  determinism and boundary-near stability (2). Sub-tests accumulate; single
  failures cost only their sub-test.
- Output contract O (5): all-or-nothing mechanical check of the three
  artifacts.

Score caps, all applied simultaneously (final = min of raw score and every
applicable cap): missing/empty/unrecognizable ANALYSIS.md → 39; missing or
unrunnable solver, or confirmed lookup/hardcoding → 49; C1 failed or C6
failed → 59; fewer than 4 checkpoints passed → 59; N < 15 → 59; O = 0 → 59.

Numerical comparison bounds (absolute unless stated): optimized Bell values
1e-3 (2e-3 for permutation-invariance consistency, 5e-3 for the
near-degenerate stability probe); entanglement quantities 5e-7 (F3 2e-6);
correlation-tensor entries 1e-7; states and amplitude vectors by projective
fidelity 1 − F ≤ 1e-9; certificate bridge artifacts 1e-6 relative to scale;
amplitude components are treated as zero below 1e-8 of the vector's largest
component; determinism repeats must agree to 1e-9. Tolerances were
calibrated so that a correct implementation passes with orders-of-magnitude
margin; they are far below the error scale of any wrong formula or missing
optimization.

# Infer a finite-horizon poisoning balance from catalytic-lattice KMC

## Scientific background

Consider the irreversible surface reaction

```text
A(g) + B(g) → AB(g).
```

The gas reservoir has fixed composition: `X_A` is the mole fraction of A and
`1-X_A` is the mole fraction of B. These are reservoir fractions, not surface
coverages. The surface fractions are `theta_A`, `theta_B`, and `theta_empty`.

Adsorption occurs only after an impact on an empty site and then only with the
species- and material-dependent sticking probability. Neighbouring unlike
adsorbates react and desorb immediately. Unequal effective adsorption supplies
therefore shift the competition between an absorbing A-covered surface and an
absorbing B-covered surface.

On a finite stochastic lattice, a trajectory can remain reactive for a long
time and still poison later. Survival to the requested horizon is
right-censoring, not evidence of an eternal steady state.

Your task is to estimate a finite-horizon A/B poisoning balance from genuine
stochastic simulation, test effective-supply predictions on monometallic and
checkerboard-bimetallic surfaces, and assess one matched finite-size
comparison. The problem is self-contained; no source paper is required.

## Input contract and visible instance

Your submission must implement the executable interface specified below. For
the visible run, materialize the exact JSON instance embedded in this
instruction and pass its path as `INPUT_JSON`. Its top-level `cases` list is in
authoritative input order. The top-level `bootstrap_replicates` is the
requested resample count when you choose a bootstrap estimator. Every case
supplies:

- `case_id`, `execution_class`, `surface_type`;
- `lattice_size=L`, `max_cycles=T`, `late_window_cycles`, and
  `record_cycles`;
- a `parameters` object;
- an ordered `x_a_grid`;
- `seed_base`, `replicates`, and `bootstrap_seed`;
- `prediction_split`, equal to `fit`, `holdout`, or `gate`;
- optional `anchor_group` and `label_exchange_group`.

For composition index `x_index` in the input `x_a_grid` and zero-based
`replicate_index`, the trajectory seed is exactly

```text
seed = seed_base + 1000*x_index + replicate_index.
```

Run every requested `(case, X_A, seed)` once. Do not sort the grid before
deriving seeds. All trajectories must use
`numpy.random.Generator(numpy.random.PCG64(seed))`; production is compared
statistically, while canaries are replayed exactly. If your uncertainty method
uses stochastic resampling, seed it with the case's `bootstrap_seed`.
The guaranteed runtime is Python 3.10 with NumPy 2.1.3.

The universal checker will freeze your entry point and invoke it once with an
undisclosed JSON instance that follows exactly the same schema but contains
different case IDs and parameter values. Do not hard-code visible case IDs,
case order, grids, parameters, row counts, or expected numerical results.

### Visible input

```json
{
  "schema_version": "2.0",
  "bootstrap_replicates": 300,
  "cases": [
    {
      "case_id": "public-kernel-canary",
      "study_role": "event_kernel_gate",
      "prediction_split": "gate",
      "execution_class": "deterministic_canary",
      "surface_type": "monometallic",
      "lattice_size": 4,
      "max_cycles": 4,
      "late_window_cycles": 2,
      "record_cycles": [
        1,
        2,
        4
      ],
      "parameters": {
        "s_a": 0.6,
        "s_b": 0.4
      },
      "x_a_grid": [
        0.5
      ],
      "seed_base": 202607280000,
      "replicates": 1,

## Frozen microscopic model

The surface is an initially empty periodic `L×L` square lattice. A site is
encoded as empty, A, or B. One Monte Carlo cycle is `L²` impact attempts.

For each impact:

1. Draw one site uniformly from all `L²` sites.
2. If it is occupied, end the impact without drawing a species or sticking
   variate.
3. At an empty site, draw A with probability `X_A`, otherwise B. Count this as
   an A or B arrival.
4. Draw adsorption acceptance using the chosen species' sticking probability
   on that fixed site type. Count a successful acceptance as an adsorption.
5. After adsorption, enumerate unlike axial neighbours in the order left,
   right, up, down, with periodic wrapping.
6. If at least one unlike neighbour exists, choose one uniformly, remove it
   and the new adsorbate, and count exactly one reaction. If there is exactly
   one unlike neighbour, select it without another random draw.

For a monometallic surface the coefficients are `s_a` for A and `s_b` for B.

For a bimetallic surface, `L` is even. Site `a` has
`(row+column) mod 2 == 0`; site `b` has odd parity. In `s_ij`, the first
subscript is adsorbing species and the second is site type:

```text
             site a          site b
species A      s_aa       s_ab = 1-s_bb
species B  s_ba = 1-s_aa      s_bb
```

This checkerboard and complementarity are assumptions of this task, not a
universal catalyst law.

The lattice poisons immediately when an impact leaves all sites occupied by
one species. Stop that trajectory at once. If poisoning occurs on the `k`-th
impact of one-based cycle `c`, record

```text
poisoning_cycle = completed_cycles = (c-1) + k/L².
```

An unpoisoned run stops after cycle `T`, with `completed_cycles=T`.

## Observables and units

Use the following canonical categories:

- `poison_species`: `A`, `B`, or the empty string for a censored run;
- `state`: `active`, `right_censored`, `poisoned_a`, or `poisoned_b`;
- `balance_status`: `resolved` or `unresolved`;
- booleans: JSON/CSV boolean values such as `true` and `false`.

`time_series.csv` must contain the end-of-cycle state for each requested
`record_cycles` value that the trajectory reaches. Always include the terminal
row: cycle `T` for a survivor or the fractional poisoning time for a poisoned
run, even when that time was not requested. Do not add synthetic rows after
poisoning. If the previous emitted time is `t_0`, define

```text
window_reaction_rate
  = reactions accumulated on (t_0,t] / (L² * (t-t_0)).
```

`late_reaction_rate` uses the last
`min(late_window_cycles, number of reached cycle slices)` slices, including a
final fractional slice, and is total reactions divided by `L²` times their
total duration. Both rates therefore have units reactions per site per Monte
Carlo cycle.

At each `X_A`, aggregate the seed outcomes as follows:

```text
p_a_poisoned       = n_A / n
p_b_poisoned       = n_B / n
d_poisoning        = (n_A - n_B) / n
survival_probability = n_censored / n
restricted_mean_lifetime = mean(min(poisoning_cycle, T)).
```

`se_d_poisoning` is the ordinary sample standard error of outcome codes
`+1` (A poison), `-1` (B poison), and `0` (censored). Other `se_*` fields are
ordinary sample standard errors of the named seed-level quantities. Use an
explicit justified 95% interval for survival (Wilson is acceptable) and for
the balance.

For a canary checkpoint, set `state_sha256` to the SHA-256 of the row-major
lattice bytes after encoding empty/A/B as unsigned bytes `0/1/2`; write
lowercase hexadecimal.
`checkpoints.csv` contains one row for each emitted deterministic-canary
time-series row in the supplied input. Statistical-production cases do not
produce checkpoint rows.

## Scientific estimand

For fixed `L`, horizon `T`, and composition `x`, define

```text
D_L,T(x)
  = P(A-poisoned by T | X_A=x)
  - P(B-poisoned by T | X_A=x).
```

The simulation-derived apparent balance is a negative-to-positive crossing of
`D_L,T(x)=0`. Estimate it from the independent outcomes and give an uncertainty
interval. You may use bootstrap plus monotone regression, a binomial model, or
another justified method. Report `bracket_low` and `bracket_high` as simulated
compositions supporting the crossing. `x_grid_resolution` is the minimum
positive spacing in the case's sorted grid.

If the observed outcomes do not support a crossing, report `unresolved` and
leave the simulated balance, its interval, bracket, and every corresponding
prediction residual blank. Never substitute a theoretical value. Survival and
late reaction activity are required diagnostics, not alternative definitions
of the balance. For tied diagnostic maxima, use the smallest `X_A`.

## Research questions

### 1. Monometallic effective supply

Start from

```text
J_A proportional to X_A s_a
J_B proportional to (1-X_A) s_b.
```

Derive a balance hypothesis by equating the supplies. Compare it with the
simulation-derived balances for symmetric and asymmetric sticking pairs and
explain the direction of the shift and finite-horizon limitations.

### 2. Checkerboard bimetallic model

Construct and freeze before interpreting holdouts:

- a simple one-channel, pooled-site, or mean-sticking baseline; and
- a site-resolved effective-supply prediction that respects the two
  sublattices and the four sticking channels above.

The final site-resolved formula is deliberately not supplied. Deriving a
physically consistent rule and using it on unseen parameter combinations is
part of the research task. For every bimetallic case, report both predictions,
compare their residuals, and test:

- label exchange: paired cases sharing `label_exchange_group` must transform
  consistently under A/B exchange;
- homogeneous limit: when `s_aa+s_bb=1`, both site types present the same
  sticking coefficient to each species.

### 3. Matched finite-size robustness

Cases sharing an `anchor_group` form a matched comparison. Sticking
parameters, horizon, grid, and replicate count are fixed; only `L` changes.
Compare estimates and intervals without claiming a thermodynamic-limit
extrapolation.

## Structured prediction conventions

Use one `model_predictions.csv` row per required model and production case:

- monometallic: `prediction_role=primary`;
- bimetallic simple model: `prediction_role=baseline`;
- bimetallic sublattice model: `prediction_role=site_resolved`.

Copy `prediction_split` to `fit_or_holdout`. Set
`residual = x_balance_simulated - x_balance_predicted`. Use
`pass`, `fail`, or `not_applicable` for the two check columns. Model IDs and
parameter summaries are descriptive and may use your own names.

## Submission interface

Create an executable

/app/run_submission.sh INPUT_JSON OUTPUT_DIR
```

that works from any current directory and writes:

```

The checker will use a different input path and a fresh output directory, so
the entry point must honor both arguments and must not depend on the current

The exact columns and machine-readable output contract are embedded in the

In `run_manifest.json`, use `kmc-catalytic-sticking-v004` as `task_id`;
`input_sha256` is the SHA-256 of the exact input bytes; `code_sha256` is the

`seed_count` is the number of trajectory rows; and `output_sha256` maps every

## Deterministic canary gate

Cases marked `deterministic_canary` are an unscored event-kernel eligibility
gate. Each required variate is the next scalar `rng.random()`. Map a site draw

topicContent:
# Infer a finite-horizon poisoning balance from catalytic-lattice KMC

## Scientific background

Consider the irreversible surface reaction

```text
A(g) + B(g) → AB(g).
```

The gas reservoir has fixed composition: `X_A` is the mole fraction of A and
`1-X_A` is the mole fraction of B. These are reservoir fractions, not surface
coverages. The surface fractions are `theta_A`, `theta_B`, and `theta_empty`.

Adsorption occurs only after an impact on an empty site and then only with the
species- and material-dependent sticking probability. Neighbouring unlike
adsorbates react and desorb immediately. Unequal effective adsorption supplies
therefore shift the competition between an absorbing A-covered surface and an
absorbing B-covered surface.

On a finite stochastic lattice, a trajectory can remain reactive for a long
time and still poison later. Survival to the requested horizon is
right-censoring, not evidence of an eternal steady state.

Your task is to estimate a finite-horizon A/B poisoning balance from genuine
stochastic simulation, test effective-supply predictions on monometallic and
checkerboard-bimetallic surfaces, and assess one matched finite-size
comparison. The problem is self-contained; no source paper is required.

## Input contract and visible instance

Your submission must implement the executable interface specified below. For
the visible run, materialize the exact JSON instance embedded in this
instruction and pass its path as `INPUT_JSON`. Its top-level `cases` list is in
authoritative input order. The top-level `bootstrap_replicates` is the
requested resample count when you choose a bootstrap estimator. Every case
supplies:

- `case_id`, `execution_class`, `surface_type`;
- `lattice_size=L`, `max_cycles=T`, `late_window_cycles`, and
  `record_cycles`;
- a `parameters` object;
- an ordered `x_a_grid`;
- `seed_base`, `replicates`, and `bootstrap_seed`;
- `prediction_split`, equal to `fit`, `holdout`, or `gate`;

For composition index `x_index` in the input `x_a_grid` and zero-based
`replicate_index`, the trajectory seed is exactly

```text
seed = seed_base + 1000*x_index + replicate_index.
```
